object-creation.role: Assemble one complex object in steps
object-creation.tour: Drive the builder through small named steps and ask it for the finished product, instead of one constructor taking every field. It is the alternative to a family factory when you want one product built in steps, and named steps make an unexpected argument order impossible.
object-creation.fluency: Construct a complex object step by step instead of one huge constructor.

object-creation.tour: Each object knows how to clone itself, so the client asks an example for a copy of the right concrete type without naming it. A family factory can clone registered prototypes instead of newing them.
object-creation.fluency: Make new objects by copying an existing instance.

object-creation.tour: The class hides its constructor, keeps the sole instance in a static field and hands it out through an accessor. It answers how many instances exist, and it costs you a global, which the next steps offer ways around.
object-creation.fluency: Permit only one instance of a class and give it a well-known access point.

object-creation.role: One shared state behind ordinary instances
object-creation.tour: Every instance looks independent but all data sits in static storage, so any instance reads and writes the one shared copy. It is often confused with a singleton, which makes the sharing explicit instead.
object-creation.fluency: Share one set of values across every instance of a class.

object-creation.tour: An accessor checks whether the value exists, creates and stores it if not, and returns the cached one afterwards. It is the classic way a single instance is created, and it spares you the cost when the value is never needed.
object-creation.fluency: Defer building a value until the first moment it is needed.

object-creation.role: Look collaborators up in a registry
object-creation.tour: A central object holds shared services keyed by type or name, and a class calls get at the point of use. It is the pull alternative to injection, and it hides what the class depends on from its signature.
object-creation.fluency: Fetch shared services from a central registry when you need them.

object-creation.tour: The class declares what it needs, usually as an interface, and an outside party supplies the instance, so it never calls new on a collaborator or reaches into a global. It is the alternative to a singleton or a locator, and it is what lets a test substitute a stand-in.
object-creation.fluency: Pass an object its dependencies instead of letting it create or find them.

object-structure.role: Convert the interface you have into the one you need
object-structure.tour: A class implements the target interface and forwards each call to the adaptee, translating names, argument shapes and return values. It fixes a mismatch after the fact, where a bridge designs the split up front.
object-structure.fluency: Make an incompatible object fit the interface a client expects.

object-structure.role: Split two concerns into two hierarchies
object-structure.tour: The abstraction holds a reference to an implementation, and that reference is the bridge. Either side extends without touching the other, which avoids a subclass for every combination, and a factory can choose the implementor.
object-structure.fluency: Separate an abstraction from its implementation so each varies alone.

object-structure.tour: A wrapper has the same interface as the thing it wraps and adds behaviour before or after the forwarded call. Callers cannot tell the layers apart, and stacking works because each wrapper stays substitutable for the original.
object-structure.fluency: Add behaviour to an object by wrapping it in one with the same interface.

object-structure.tour: A stand-in with the same interface that can check permissions, create the subject lazily, cache a result or ship the call elsewhere. It has the same shape as a decorator, but it controls access where a decorator adds behaviour.
object-structure.fluency: Stand in front of an object to control or defer access to it.

object-behavior.role: Swap the algorithm the caller picks
object-behavior.tour: A family of algorithms behind one interface, and the context holds a reference and delegates without knowing which one. It is the textbook way to be open to new behaviour and closed to modification, and it is a direct application of holding a behaviour instead of inheriting it.
object-behavior.fluency: Put each algorithm behind one interface and let the client pick.

object-behavior.role: Change behaviour as the object's own state changes
object-behavior.tour: The context holds a state object and delegates to it, and each concrete state is a class implementing the same interface. One call does something different depending on which state is plugged in. It is often confused with strategy, which swaps an algorithm rather than following state.
object-behavior.fluency: Let an object change what it does when its internal state changes.

object-behavior.role: Fix the skeleton, let subclasses fill the steps
object-behavior.tour: One method in a base class calls a fixed sequence of concrete steps, abstract blanks and hooks with defaults. Subclasses fill the blanks without touching the sequence. It is the subclass alternative to strategy, which composes the algorithm instead.
object-behavior.fluency: Define an algorithm's outline in a base class and defer steps to subclasses.

object-behavior.role: A do-nothing member of the family
object-behavior.tour: A real object with the same interface whose methods do nothing or return a neutral value, handed back instead of null. It is a neutral strategy, it holds no state so one shared instance serves every call site, and it is valid only where the contract allows doing nothing.
object-behavior.fluency: Return a harmless do-nothing object instead of null.

object-behavior.role: Pass the request along until someone handles it
object-behavior.tour: Handlers line up, and each deals with the request or forwards it to its successor, so the sender never knows which one answers. One handler may stop the request, which a decorator never does. A validator chain is the textbook use.
object-behavior.fluency: Send a request through a line of handlers until one deals with it.

object-behavior.tour: Colleagues know only the mediator, which decides who else must react. It centralises interactions where an observer broadcasts changes, and it is how you stop a set of objects holding references to each other.
object-behavior.fluency: Route all interaction between a set of objects through one object.

object-behavior.role: Hide how a collection is walked
object-behavior.tour: The iterator holds the traversal position and exposes a tiny protocol such as hasNext and next, so the collection never has to. On a tree it walks uniformly, and the aggregate's createIterator is a factory method for the right cursor.
object-behavior.fluency: Walk a collection one element at a time without exposing how it is stored.

object-behavior.role: Add an operation without editing the classes
object-behavior.tour: Each element exposes accept, and the visitor carries one method per element type. A new operation is a new visitor and the element classes never change. A traversal walks the structure and hands each node to the visitor.
object-behavior.fluency: Move an operation out of a class hierarchy into a separate object.

object-behavior.role: Give a small language its own tree
object-behavior.tour: One class per grammar rule, and a sentence becomes a syntax tree whose nodes each expose interpret. Evaluation is a recursive call from the root. The tree is a composite, repeated terminal symbols can be shared, and visitors evaluate it.
object-behavior.fluency: Model a small language as a tree of rule objects and evaluate it recursively.

object-behavior.role: Save a snapshot you can restore
object-behavior.tour: The originator snapshots its state into an opaque memento, and a caretaker holds mementos without looking inside. Command does and memento captures the state to undo, and immutable snapshots make undo trivial.
object-behavior.fluency: Capture an object's state in a separate object so you can restore it later.

consistency-and-replication.tour: When replicas take writes on their own, a plain timestamp cannot say whether one write came before another or beside it. Each replica keeps a counter per replica, and comparing two sets of counters shows an older version or a true conflict. You pay a counter per replica on every value, and a conflict still needs a rule to resolve it.
consistency-and-replication.fluency: Per-replica counters tell an older version from a concurrent one, so no update is silently dropped when replicas take writes alone.

consistency-and-replication.tour: Instead of detecting conflicts and resolving them, build the merge into the data type so replicas that took writes alone converge in any order, with repeats. You give up rules that span replicas, and some types grow memory over time.
consistency-and-replication.fluency: A merge built into the data type lets replicas take writes alone and still converge.

consistency-and-replication.role: Promote a standby when the primary dies, and fence the old one.
consistency-and-replication.tour: Replication keeps a copy, and failover is what uses it when a node fails: detect the failure, fence the old primary, promote a standby and redirect clients. The lag window is the data you can lose, and a wrong detection is how two primaries appear.
consistency-and-replication.fluency: What replication is for when a node fails: detect, fence, promote, redirect, with the lag window as the data you can lose.

consistency-and-replication.tour: Copies drift even when every write is sent to all of them. Two replicas compare hashes from the root of a tree down, and only the ranges whose hashes differ are exchanged. Repair costs a scan of the changed ranges instead of the whole data set, and the tree must be kept up to date as writes land.
consistency-and-replication.fluency: Compares hashes down a tree to find the few ranges two replicas disagree on, so repair does not scan everything.

scale-units-and-stamps.tour: Tenants can share rows, share a database, or each get a whole stamp, and the choice trades cost against isolation. A catalog of where each tenant lives lets you move a tenant to a stronger model later. The price is a noisy tenant in the shared models and an operations bill in the isolated ones.
scale-units-and-stamps.fluency: The isolation models run from shared rows to a stamp per tenant, and a catalog lets you move a tenant between them.

enterprise-application-patterns.role: Name a business rule once and reuse it to check and to query
enterprise-application-patterns.tour: A specification wraps one business rule in an object that answers match or no match, and and, or and not join specifications into bigger rules. A repository can test it in memory or turn it into a query, so the rule is written once. Translating to a query is the part that grows hard.
enterprise-application-patterns.fluency: Express a rule as a composable predicate that a repository can test or turn into a query.

enterprise-application-patterns.role: Keep one object per row inside a unit of work
enterprise-application-patterns.tour: Without a map, two loads of one row give two objects that disagree. The identity map is checked by key before every load, so a unit of work holds one object per row and writes each changed row once. The map is a stale view during a long unit, so pair it with a version check on save.
enterprise-application-patterns.fluency: Check a map by key before every load, so two reads of one row give one object.

realtime-updates.role: The simplest push over plain HTTP
realtime-updates.tour: The entry that needs no new infrastructure. The client holds a request open until news or a timeout, then asks again, so any proxy and any client works. Choose it for occasional updates, or as the fallback when a better transport is blocked, and accept a request per message.
realtime-updates.fluency: Hold a request open until there is news

realtime-updates.tour: One long-lived HTTP response the server writes events down. The browser reconnects by itself and resumes from the last event id, so feeds, dashboards and streamed artificial intelligence (AI) answers need no protocol work. The limit is one direction and text only.
realtime-updates.fluency: One-way stream over plain HTTP with built-in reconnect

realtime-updates.role: Two-way connection for chat and editing
realtime-updates.tour: When both sides send often, upgrade the connection to full duplex. The socket lives on one server, so every event for the user needs a bus or sticky routing to reach it, and reconnect, replay and slow-client limits are yours to build.
realtime-updates.fluency: Two-way connection that the infrastructure must hold open

microservices-design.role: Keep a local copy instead of calling the owner
microservices-design.tour: Once data ownership is split, consumers still need other services' data. Put the changed state inside the event so each consumer keeps its own copy and reads it locally, which removes the callback and the runtime coupling at the price of seconds of staleness and a shared event contract.
microservices-design.fluency: Events carry the data so consumers keep a local copy

resilience.role: Return a reduced answer when the call fails
resilience.tour: When the call is cut short by a timeout, a breaker or a full bulkhead, the caller still has to show something. A fallback picks the lesser answer, such as a cached value or a default, for that one request. Decide it in advance, or the user sees a plain error.
resilience.fluency: Decides what the user sees once a breaker or timeout has cut the call short

resilience.role: Beat a slow replica, not just a failed one
resilience.tour: A retry waits for a failure, which never comes when a replica is only slow. Send a second copy to another replica after a short delay and take the first answer. It needs a call that is safe to repeat and a cap on the share of hedged requests, since extra copies add load.
resilience.fluency: Answers lateness where retries only answer failure, at the price of a few percent extra load

resilience.role: Notice a silent failure with a timed alive signal and a timeout.
resilience.tour: A node that crashes says nothing, so silence is the only signal. A heartbeat is a small message sent on a timer, and a missed run of them is a suspicion that the node is gone. Set the timeout against your pauses, or a slow node is declared dead.
resilience.fluency: The liveness signal behind election, failover and lease renewal, which gives a suspicion and never a fact.

spike-handling.role: Smooth the output to a fixed rate
spike-handling.tour: Requests join a queue of fixed size and leave at a fixed rate, so a burst becomes waiting and the target never sees a spike. When the queue is full the rest are refused. You pay in delay for the requests that wait.
spike-handling.fluency: The strict twin of the token bucket: bursts become waiting, so a fragile target never sees a spike

dealing-with-contention.role: Make the lock expire on its own: a time-bound grant the holder must renew.
dealing-with-contention.tour: A lease is a grant that ends at a deadline unless the holder renews it. A holder that crashes frees the resource when the deadline passes, with no cleanup job. A paused holder can still act after expiry, so pair it with a check at the resource.
dealing-with-contention.fluency: The time-bound core of a distributed lock: a crashed holder frees the resource at the deadline, with no cleanup job.

dealing-with-contention.role: Make the resource refuse a late writer: a rising number checked on every write.
dealing-with-contention.tour: Each grant of the lock carries a number that rises, and the resource refuses any write with a lower number than one it has seen. A paused holder that wakes after its lease ended is refused, whatever the clocks say. The resource must be able to do the check.
dealing-with-contention.fluency: The check that stays safe when a paused holder wakes after its lease expired: its older number is refused.

multi-step-processes.role: The atomic baseline: all participants commit or none, at the price of blocking.
multi-step-processes.tour: Every participant votes on whether it can commit, and only then does the coordinator tell all of them to commit. Nobody ends half done. Locks stay held while the votes come in, and a coordinator that dies blocks the prepared participants, which is the cost the saga avoids.
multi-step-processes.fluency: Why a saga exists: two-phase commit holds locks across services and blocks when the coordinator dies.

scaling-reads.role: Serve keyword reads from a term-to-document index
scaling-reads.tour: Reads for a keyword never scan the documents. The index lists the documents for each term, so the read touches only those lists and write cost is paid once at indexing time.
scaling-reads.fluency: Answer keyword searches from a prebuilt term-to-document index instead of scanning.

proximity-search.tour: A prefix tree finds every cell or term that starts with a given prefix by walking one path. Paired with a geohash, the shared prefix means the same neighbourhood.
proximity-search.fluency: Look up everything under a prefix by walking one path of a tree.

continuous-validation.tour: Instances are swapped in place a batch at a time with no second fleet. The roll can pause after the first batch and be judged like a canary before it continues.
continuous-validation.fluency: Replace running instances in small batches so some always serve traffic.

continuous-validation.role: Test a new version on mirrored live requests
continuous-validation.tour: Real requests are copied to the new version and its responses are thrown away, so no user sees it. You compare its answers and timing against the old version before any real traffic moves.
continuous-validation.fluency: Copy live requests to a new version and discard its replies to test it safely.

service-boundaries.tour: Once the contexts exist, a map names the relationship on each border: who is upstream, who translates, and which model is shared.
service-boundaries.fluency: Record how each pair of bounded contexts relates on a single map.

service-boundaries.tour: A rule that belongs to no single aggregate or entity lives in a stateless service in the domain, so the boundaries stay clean.
service-boundaries.fluency: Put a rule that spans several aggregates in a stateless domain service.

api-design.role: Route every request through one entry point
api-design.tour: One handler receives every request, runs the shared steps and dispatches to the right controller. An application programming interface (API) gateway is the same idea across services.
api-design.fluency: Send every request through one handler that applies shared steps and dispatches.

enterprise-application-patterns.role: Express a search as an object
enterprise-application-patterns.tour: The caller builds criteria as an object and the repository or mapper turns it into a query, so callers need no SQL and the storage stays hidden.
enterprise-application-patterns.fluency: Describe an open-ended search as an object that a repository turns into a query.

concurrency.role: Give state one thread behind typed method calls
concurrency.tour: Calls become queued requests that one scheduler thread runs, and each returns a future. Callers never take a lock, and state stays owned by one thread.
concurrency.fluency: Hand method calls to one owning thread through a queue and get futures back.

concurrency.role: Pass values between tasks through a queue
concurrency.tour: Tasks hand values to each other through a bounded channel, so ownership moves with the value and a full buffer slows the sender.
concurrency.fluency: Pass values between tasks through a bounded channel instead of sharing memory.

concurrency.role: Let the system finish the I/O first
concurrency.tour: The operating system completes the read or write and hands the finished result to a handler, so no thread waits while the I/O runs.
concurrency.fluency: Start I/O and get called back with the finished result.

concurrency.role: Skip the lock on the fast path of lazy creation
concurrency.tour: Check for the object without a lock, then lock and check again before creating it. It is subtle: it needs a memory barrier to be correct.
concurrency.fluency: Avoid taking a lock on every read of a lazily created value, and know why it is subtle.

streaming.role: Use a fixed circular array as the queue
streaming.tour: A fixed circular array sits between producer and consumer, with a policy for when it is full, so it never grows and allocates nothing per item.
streaming.fluency: Hold the queue between a producer and a consumer in a fixed circular array.

message-flow.tour: Messages that arrive out of order are held until the gap fills, then released in sequence. Each message passes on unchanged.
message-flow.fluency: Put out-of-order messages back in sequence before passing them on.

message-flow.role: Add data the message does not carry
message-flow.tour: The step fetches missing data from another source and merges it into the message, so later steps get what they need without a lookup of their own.
message-flow.fluency: Add missing data to a message by fetching it from another source in flight.

message-flow.role: Let the route travel with the message
message-flow.tour: An ordered list of steps rides with the message and each processor forwards it to the next address on the slip, so no central router knows every route.
message-flow.fluency: Attach the list of steps to a message so each processor forwards it to the next.

long-running-tasks.role: Pull work when you have capacity
long-running-tasks.tour: The consumer asks the queue for the next message only when it is free, so it sets its own pace and a burst waits in the queue.
long-running-tasks.fluency: Pull the next message only when ready, so the consumer sets the pace.

message-flow.tour: Each application translates to and from one shared format instead of to every other application, so n applications need n translators, not n squared.
message-flow.fluency: Translate every application to one shared format instead of to each other.

concurrency.role: Let one thread at a time change shared data
concurrency.tour: A lock with an owner guards the shared data, so two threads cannot interleave their reads and writes. Every other caller waits its turn.
concurrency.fluency: Guard shared data with a lock so one thread at a time changes it.

concurrency.role: Make every thread finish a phase together
concurrency.tour: Threads wait at a barrier until all arrive, so no thread starts the next phase before every thread has finished the last.
concurrency.fluency: Hold every thread at a point until all have arrived before any goes on.

concurrency.role: Split a job, run the pieces, merge the results
concurrency.tour: A job splits into small pieces that run on a pool, often with work stealing, then the join waits for them and merges the results.
concurrency.fluency: Split work into pieces, run them in parallel and merge the results.
